claims.text: The starting AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy has a uniform, fine lamellar microstructure.
The intervention consists of cryogenic rolling followed by warm rolling at 600 °C.
The cryogenic-rolling stage imparts a strain of approximately 1.2.
The warm-rolling stage imparts an additional strain of approximately 1.2.
Hybrid rolling produces a heterogeneous microstructure containing retained lamellar regions and transformed nanocrystalline regions.
Cryogenic rolling stores deformation energy that accelerates transformations during subsequent low-temperature warm rolling.
The warm-rolling stage precipitates nanocrystalline regions in the matrix.
The nanocrystalline regions create numerous high-angle interfaces.
The resulting interfaces impede dislocation movement.
The resulting interfaces reduce grain-boundary sliding and thereby slow room-temperature creep.
Hybrid processing alters interfacial chemistry in a way that can improve corrosion resistance.
The hybrid-rolled heterogeneous microstructure improves the strength–ductility balance relative to the conventional uniform lamellar alloy.
The hybrid-rolled alloy will have a lower room-temperature creep rate under long-term loading than the conventional alloy.
The hybrid-rolled alloy will have better corrosion resistance under extreme temperature fluctuations than the conventional alloy.
Producing the desired heterogeneous structure depends on precise control of rolling strain and temperature.
Processing deviations may produce unstable interfaces during repetitive temperature cycling.
The required volume fraction and spatial distribution of nanocrystalline and lamellar regions for optimal creep and corrosion performance are not established.
The long-term stability of the hybrid-rolled microstructure under combined mechanical and thermal stresses remains unvalidated.
